spots.name: Fallingwater
spots.label: Fallingwater

text.access_note: Fallingwater is a ticketed house museum run as a visitor attraction, so check the official site before you go for tours, entry and which areas of the grounds you can visit.
text.directions_text: Fallingwater is near Pennsylvania Route 381, between Ohiopyle and Mill Run, about 72 miles (116 km) south-east of Pittsburgh. The visitor pavilion is the starting point on site; follow the paths from there towards the house. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description: Fallingwater is a house museum in the Laurel Highlands of southwestern Pennsylvania, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright as a weekend retreat for Edgar J. Kaufmann Sr. and his wife Liliane. It is built partly over a waterfall on the Bear Run stream. Its long concrete terraces are cantilevered, reaching out from a chimney with no support at the far end. That gives you strong horizontal lines to set against the rock, the trees and the moving water. The house is made of locally quarried stone, reinforced concrete, steel and plate glass, so the textures also reward a closer look. The Kaufmanns began using the house in 1937, and the Western Pennsylvania Conservancy has run it as a visitor attraction since 1963. It is a National Historic Landmark and part of a World Heritage Site. The house sits under a canopy of forest and is not on a prominent hilltop, so expect dappled light and a lot of green around it. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m north-west of the subject. That is close enough to fit the main block in one frame with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x), and to pick out terraces and stonework with the zoom. Take a wide shot first, then a few tighter ones. The stream can freeze in winter and dry up in summer, so the waterfall will not always look the same.
text.geographic_location: Fallingwater stands in Stewart Township, Fayette County, above the Bear Run stream, between the communities of Ohiopyle and Mill Run.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky and water do not wash out. If the light is patchy, take two or three shots and keep the best. A Live Photo can catch moving leaves or water. Use panorama only if you can move slowly and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the long terrace edges with them so the horizontal lines stay level. Keep a little of the surrounding trees and rock in the frame to show how the house sits in the landscape. Try one wide shot and one tighter shot of the terraces. Hold your phone steady against a rail or tree if one is nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole house and its terraces from this close. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the stonework, the glass and the edges of the terraces.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 40 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Take a few steps to either side if trees block part of the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light on an overcast day suits the stonework and green canopy, with less harsh dappled shadow. Whenever you go, check the official site for visiting times before you set out.

spots.name: Kentuck Knob
spots.label: Kentuck Knob

text.access_note: The house is open to the public for tours, and it is not clear whether the overlook or hillside areas can be used without a tour ticket, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: There is no public transport stop nearby. The house is reached by road, along a long gravel driveway from Pennsylvania Route 2010, which runs through woods. Fallingwater is about a 7-mile drive to the northeast of Kentuck Knob, so from Fallingwater head south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description:
Kentuck Knob is a small house designed by Frank Lloyd Wright for I. N. Hagan, an ice-cream company owner, and his wife Bernardine. It was completed in 1956 and sits on the southern slope of a wooded knoll. The walls are locally quarried stone and redwood, with a broad overhanging copper roof, and the plan is built around a hexagon. It is a National Historic Landmark. The house is a few miles from Fallingwater, and the Hagans first heard of Wright through the family who built Fallingwater.

It photographs well because the low roofline and the stone seem to grow out of the hillside. The best exterior view is usually from the back. From the informal overlook on the east side of the house, about 100 m south-east of it, you see the sandstone walls and the cantilevered roof, with the Youghiogheny River gorge and Laurel Highlands ridges behind. Trees can screen the gorge itself, so expect the ridges and treetops to do most of the work in the background. The entrance side, with the carport and the roofline set into the hill, is a good second shot. So is a side view from higher up the hillside, framed by trees.

No photography is allowed inside the house, so plan on outdoor pictures only.
text.geographic_location: Kentuck Knob is in Stewart Township, Fayette County, Pennsylvania, a few miles from Fallingwater rather than in the town itself. The house stands on the southern slope of a wooded knoll above the Youghiogheny River gorge.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone wall to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky and ridges keep some colour. If the roof overhang makes the walls too dark, tap the shaded wall and raise the exposure slightly. Try a panorama only if you can keep the phone steady and level.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the roofline along the upper third, with the ridges above it. Keep the horizon level, since the long horizontal roof shows any tilt. For a different view, try the entrance side with the carport, or a side view from the hillside framed by trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the house and ridges together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the roof gets cut off. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the stone and the copper roof edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kentuck Knob Overlook (a few steps from the back terrace, on the east side of the house). The house's rear side with its sandstone walls and cantilevered roof, with the Youghiogheny River gorge and Laurel Highlands ridges behind it. From here the house lies to the north-west. You see its rear side with the sandstone walls and cantilevered roof, and the gorge and ridges behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light on a bright overcast day suits the stone and the copper roof, because it avoids hard shadows under the overhang. Autumn leaf colour could add warmth to the trees around the house.

spots.name: Ohiopyle State Park
spots.label: Ohiopyle State Park

text.access_note: The falls area is part of a state park with public viewing decks; check the official site before you go for current access, construction and parking.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot. Start from the village of Ohiopyle and head for the parking lot on Main Street (Route 381). The observation decks are right beside that parking lot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description: Ohiopyle State Park covers about 20,500 acres of forested gorge country in Fayette County, Pennsylvania, and Ohiopyle Falls is its best-known sight. The falls are only about 20 feet (6 m) high, but they stretch right across the Youghiogheny River, so the picture is all about width and moving white water. The name comes from a Lenape phrase meaning 'it turns very white', which suits the frothy water. Guides call this the most photographed spot in the park. From the Ohiopyle Falls Observation Deck you look across the full width of the falls, with the tree-covered Ferncliff Peninsula behind. The deck is beside the parking lot on Main Street (Route 381), so it is the easiest viewpoint to reach. The park opened to the public in 1965 and was formally dedicated in 1971. It sits on the site of old railway-age resorts that drew visitors to the falls. For a different angle, Baughman Rock Overlook gives long views down the river gorge, and the Ohiopyle High Bridge looks down on the rapids through its arches. Kayakers sometimes run the rapids below. Take a few wide shots first, then move in for details of the water. The falls area was reported as being rebuilt, so check current construction and parking before you go.
text.geographic_location: This spot is in the village of Ohiopyle, in the Falls Day Use Area at the centre of Ohiopyle State Park, beside the parking lot on Main Street (Route 381). It is several miles from the Fallingwater house itself.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest white water to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the foam keeps its detail. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the water. Wipe your lens first, as spray may smear it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the lip of the falls along a lower line, so the water fills the frame and the trees sit above it. Try one wide shot and one tighter zoomed shot. If you have time, Baughman Rock Overlook is a good second viewpoint for long gorge views.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole width of the falls and the forest behind. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the white water or the trees of Ferncliff Peninsula.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (observation decks beside the parking lot on Main Street / Route 381). The full width of Ohiopyle Falls spanning the Youghiogheny River, with the forested Ferncliff Peninsula behind it. You are looking at Ohiopyle Falls across the Youghiogheny River, with the forested Ferncliff Peninsula behind; the deck gives you the full width of the falls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there is less glare on the water.
